def: An AI system that works in a loop: it decides on a step, uses a tool (search, code, an API), looks at the result and decides the next step until the goal is done.
Describes software where the AI chooses its own next actions instead of following a fixed script.
A way for one program to talk to another. AI APIs let your app send a prompt to a model and get the answer back, usually paid per token.
A fixed test set used to compare models on the same tasks, such as coding or maths. Useful as a signal, but models can be tuned to score well on them.
When a model writes out intermediate reasoning steps before its final answer. It often improves results on multi-step problems.
Splitting long documents into smaller pieces before embedding them for RAG, so the right passage can be found and fit into the prompt.
How much text (in tokens) a model can take in at once, including your prompt, any documents and its own reply. Anything beyond it is cut off.
A model that creates images, audio or video by starting from random noise and removing it step by step until a picture matching the prompt appears.
Training a smaller, cheaper model to copy the outputs of a larger one, keeping much of its skill at a fraction of the cost.
A list of numbers that captures the meaning of a piece of text or an image. Similar meanings get similar numbers, which is what powers semantic search.
A repeatable test you run on your own AI app to check answers are right, safe and on-format before and after every change.
Putting a few worked examples in the prompt so the model copies the pattern. Zero-shot means no examples.
Further training a model on your own examples so it learns a style, format or narrow skill. Changes behaviour; it is a poor way to add fresh facts.
A model feature where, instead of plain text, the model returns a structured request to run one of the tools you described, with the arguments filled in.
A file format for running quantized models on ordinary computers with tools like llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio.
The chip most AI runs on. Its memory (VRAM) decides how large a model you can load locally.
Checks around a model that block unsafe inputs or outputs, such as filters, validators and allow-lists for tools.
When a model states something false with confidence. Grounding answers in sources (RAG, search) and asking for citations reduces it.
Running a trained model to get an answer. Training builds the model; inference is every time you use it.
A prompt crafted to make a model ignore its safety rules.
How long you wait for a response. For chat, time to first token matters most because answers stream in.
Large language model: a model trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token, which lets it write, summarise, translate and code.
Low-rank adaptation: a cheap fine-tuning method that trains a small add-on instead of the whole model. QLoRA does the same on a quantized model.
Model Context Protocol: an open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data. Write an MCP server once and any MCP-aware app can use it.
A model built from many sub-networks where only a few run for each token, so a very large model costs less to run.
A model that works with more than one kind of input or output, such as text plus images, audio or video.
A model whose trained weights you can download and run yourself. Not always fully open source: training data and code may stay private.
The learned numbers inside a model. More parameters usually means more capability and more memory needed (e.g. 7B = 7 billion).
The instructions and context you give a model. Clear role, task, context and output format get better answers.
An attack where text inside a web page, file or email gives the model new instructions, hijacking what it does. The top security risk for AI apps.
Storing a model's numbers with fewer bits (e.g. 4-bit) so it uses far less memory and runs on normal hardware, with a small quality loss.
Retrieval-augmented generation: search your own documents for relevant passages and put them in the prompt, so answers use your data and can cite it.
A model trained to think through a problem at length before answering. Slower and pricier per answer, stronger on maths, code and planning.
A second model that re-orders search results by how well they actually answer the question, improving RAG accuracy.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: training a model on human ratings of its answers so it becomes more helpful and safer.
Getting a model to reply in an exact format such as JSON matching a schema, so your code can read it reliably.
Standing instructions set by the app developer that shape every reply, separate from what the user types.
A setting for randomness. Low gives focused, repeatable answers; high gives more varied, creative ones.
The chunk of text a model reads and writes, roughly three-quarters of an English word. Context limits and API prices are counted in tokens.
Letting a model call outside tools such as search, a calculator, a database or code, then use the results in its answer.
The neural network design behind almost every modern LLM. Its attention mechanism lets every token look at every other token.
Text-to-speech turns text into a voice; speech-to-text (ASR) turns recorded speech into text.
A database built to store embeddings and quickly find the ones closest in meaning to a query. The search engine inside most RAG apps.
Building software by describing what you want to an AI coding tool and steering it, rather than writing most of the code yourself.
